title: Remembering the dead

segments.voice: Yesterday, Buddhist funerals, and a line about what the living can still give: merit for the dead. Did you do one small good thing in someone's name? Day one thousand four hundred nine.

A wooden cabinet stands in the corner of a living room in Japan. Inside, behind small doors, there is an image of the Buddha, a bell, a little bowl of rice, and thin lacquered tablets with names written on them. Every morning, someone in the family opens the doors, lights incense, rings the bell, and sets out fresh rice and tea. The names on the tablets belong to grandparents and great-grandparents. The names are only ink on wood. But they are greeted every morning anyway. A funeral happens once. What comes after can go on for years. Today, remembering the dead.
screen: `A CABINET IN THE LIVING ROOM.` → `NAMES ON LACQUERED TABLETS.` → `GREETED EVERY MORNING.`

segments.voice: Here are two ways Buddhist families keep the dead close: an altar at home and a day in the year. The altar comes first. In Japan it's called a butsudan, a Buddha cabinet, and the names of the family's dead are kept beside the Buddha. In Chinese and Vietnamese homes, ancestor tablets sit on a family altar. The pairing matters. The dead are not worshipped as gods. They are placed near the Buddha, and the offerings are made in the presence of the teaching. Then the day. East Asia has a yearly festival for the dead, called Obon in Japan and Yulan or the Ghost Festival in China. Its story comes from a text known as the Ullambana Sutra. A disciple of the Buddha, Maudgalyayana, known in the texts for his powers, looks for his dead mother and finds her reborn as a hungry ghost, starving. He offers her a bowl of rice, and it bursts into flame before it reaches her mouth. He runs to the Buddha. The Buddha tells him that his own power is not enough. At the end of the rainy-season retreat, he should make offerings to the whole community of monks, for the sake of his mother and his ancestors. He does, and in the story his mother is freed. So the yearly rite is not a single person's effort. It's a family, a community, a whole season of practice, all pointed at the ones who came before. In Japan, Obon is kept with lanterns and dances that welcome the dead home, and then send them off again. Remembering the dead is something done together.
screen: `AN ALTAR AT HOME.` · `NEAR THE BUDDHA, NOT AS GODS.` · `MAUDGALYAYANA AND HIS MOTHER.` · then, large: `REMEMBERED TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: If you have a candle, or even a small lamp, have it ready. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind someone who has died, maybe the same person as yesterday, maybe someone else. Say their name, silently or out loud. If you have a candle, light it now, carefully, and let it stand for them. Then just stay with the light for a while. You don't need to say anything to them, or feel any particular way. Just let the small flame keep them company while you breathe. The bell holds the time.
Remembering the dead. A home altar where the names sit near the Buddha, and a yearly rite where a whole community gives in their name. Today's word.
Your line: they are remembered. Sometime today, say the name of someone who has died to another person, and tell them one thing you remember. Day one thousand four hundred nine.

howItsDone: Buddhist families in many countries keep a home altar with the names or photographs of their dead beside an image of the Buddha, offering incense, food and light; in East Asia the yearly Obon or Ghost Festival honors ancestors with offerings to the monastic community, lanterns and gatherings.

make offerings to the whole community of monks.
accept that nothing can be done.

original.note: Pali peta (Sanskrit preta): one who has departed; also the hungry ghost Maudgalyayana's mother became.

trapdoor: what you thought: remembering the dead is private grief.
what it means: a home altar and a yearly rite, where a family and a community give in their name.
what a scholar hears: the Ullambana Sutra's story of Maudgalyayana's mother, behind Obon in Japan and the Yulan festival in China.

notes: Ullambana Sutra paraphrased: Maudgalyayana (Mulian) finds his mother as a hungry ghost; the rice turns to flame; the Buddha says his power alone is insufficient; offerings to the assembled sangha on the day the rains retreat ends (the fifteenth of the seventh month, not stated). Confirm.
'Many East Asian Buddhists keep a yearly festival' is a general claim not in the cited text; rephrased as East Asia has a yearly festival; confirm.
Butsudan contents (image, bell, rice, ihai tablets) and daily offerings are descriptive of common practice; varies by family and school. Confirm.
'The dead are not worshipped as gods' is an interpretive framing; confirm it fits Japanese and Chinese practice.
Obon lanterns and dances (welcoming and sending off the dead) described generally; confirm.
Original: Pali peta, meaning 'departed', used for hungry ghosts; confirm Devanagari and pronunciation.
Editor: softened the sweeping 'across the Buddhist world' and the general 'families' claim about Obon.
